e: The earliest and most commonly known usage of this term is in the American cartoon Scooby-Doo, where it was used regularly by one of the main characters, Norville "Shaggy" Rogers.
q: Oh Zoinks! This really smurfs things up for me! Well, at least I now know why many of my friends might feel my slang isn't as radicool as I do.
1998 March 28, David W Miller, “Re: Slang (was: REVIEW: Vampire Science)”, in rec.arts.drwho (Usenet):
After gulping hard, I said aloud, “Zoinks.” I was expecting a big black crow to peck out my eyes, or a woman to hang herself out the second story window.
2012, Michael W. Messer, Forever Sixteen, page 39:

e: Borrowed from Ancient Greek ζωϊκός (zōïkós), from ζῷον (zōîon, “animal”).
Named after Austrian scientist Baron Sigmund Zois von Edelstein (1747-1819) in 1805. + -ite
From the name of Zoilus, an ancient Greek rhetorician who severely criticized Homer's poems. From Ancient Greek Ζωΐλος (Zōḯlos).
Variant form of zooid which took on a specialised botanical meaning. By surface analysis, zoo- + -id.
Possibly from a shortening of gadzooks. Compare also yoicks.
